newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC rejects inquiry into liquor ad regulations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC rejects inquiry into liquor ad regulations.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday rejected the opening of an inquiry into whether hard liquor advertisements on radio and television should be regulated.

The commission voted 2-2 on the proposed fact-finding inquiry, which would seek public comment on the controversial issue of hard liquor broadcast advertising. A proposal needs three votes to pass the five-member commission, which currently has one vacancy.

The two FCC commissioners who opposed the inquiry, James Quello and Rachelle Chong, said they believed the matter should be handled by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which currently is investigating alleged unfair and misleading advertisements by the distilled spirits industry.
"The FCC should not get in the way of a matter beyond our authority," Quello said in the FCC meeting. "I think that it is being handled by the appropriate agency."
Commission Chairman Reed Hundt and Commissioner Susan Ness voted in favour of the proposal, which they said was backed by President (Bill) Clinton, 13 states and 240 citizens groups.

Hundt and Ness said the nonbinding inquiry would merely be a means to inform the commission on what action might be necessary in the wake of a 1993 decision by the National Association of Broadcasters to drop its self-imposed ban on hard liquor advertising. Liquor companies had refrained from advertising on radio or television on their own until 1996, and approximately 50 television stations across the country currently are broadcasting hard liquor ads, according to FCC estimates.
